meta.audience: The Amalekites of Jerusalem, and later Lamoni's people
meta.location: The Lamanite city of Jerusalem, Ani-Anti, Middoni, Ishmael
meta.unit: The sons of Mosiah among the Lamanites (Alma 17–26)
principles: Preaching where the ground is hardest

world_behind.title: This chapter backs up in time
world_behind.text: Verse 1 returns to the moment in Alma 17 when the brothers separated. Alma 20 already showed the prisoners coming out; here Mormon goes back and tells how they got in.

world_behind.title: The Lamanite Jerusalem was a settler city
world_behind.text: Verses 1 and 2 name it after the fathers' birthplace and credit three groups with building it: Lamanites, Amalekites, and the people of Amulon. Two of those three are Nephite dissenters.

world_behind.title: The dissenters were the hard core
world_behind.text: Verse 3 says the Lamanites were sufficiently hardened on their own, and that the Amalekites and Amulonites were harder and worked on them. Mormon locates the resistance in the men who left the Nephites.

world_behind.title: The order of the Nehors had gone abroad
world_behind.text: Verse 4 says the Amalekites built synagogues after that order. Nehor was executed in Alma 1 and his teaching had crossed the border and acquired buildings.

world_behind.title: Amulon's people were the priests of Noah
world_behind.text: Mosiah 23 and 24 give their history: Noah's priests, the daughters of the Lamanites, and the tyranny over Alma's people at Helam. Aaron is preaching to the descendants of the men who burned Abinadi.

world_behind.title: Aaron's route is a list of refusals
world_behind.text: The city Jerusalem, then Ani-Anti, then Middoni, then prison. Verse 12 says few believed, and Mormon records the whole itinerary at the pace it actually happened.

world_behind.title: Lamoni's grant of religious liberty is on the record
world_behind.text: Verses 21 and 22 have him telling his people they are free from his father's oppression and may worship where they wish inside his lands. The concession Ammon won in Alma 20 becomes public policy.

words.text: Birth, and by extension the place of it. The record uses the word twice, here and in Helaman 7. The Lamanites named their city after "the land of their fathers' nativity" (v. 1), which places Lehi's Jerusalem in their family memory as firmly as in the Nephites'. Both nations kept the same origin story.

cites.quote: the land of their fathers' nativity

spans.text: the land of their fathers' nativity

words.text: A body of Nephite dissenters living among the Lamanites. The name appears eighteen times in this record, all in Alma, and it is also the name of Israel's oldest enemy in the King James Bible. They are the group Aaron preaches to first and the group that later leads the slaughter of the converts in Alma 24.

Assembly houses for worship and teaching. The Amalekites built theirs "after the order of the Nehors" (v. 4), which gives a dissenting Nephite sect its own architecture in Lamanite territory. The word carries the same weight in Alma 32, where being shut out of one is what drives the poor Zoramites to Alma.

cites.quote: after the order of the Nehors

spans.text: after the order of the Nehors

words.text: Holy places, buildings set apart for worship. The Amalekite offers them as evidence of righteousness: we have built sanctuaries and we assemble in them. The record uses the word eight times, and in 2 Nephi 28 and Alma 16 it is likewise attached to people whose buildings outrun their belief.

A village between the city Jerusalem and Middoni. The name occurs once in scripture and is never explained. Mormon keeps it because Aaron found Muloki and Ammah preaching there, and the abridgment preserves the place where scattered missionaries met by accident.

Burning with eagerness for something. The record uses it four times, and the King James Bible eight, usually of men intense about the law. Mormon closes the chapter with Lamoni's people zealous for keeping the commandments, which is the outcome Aaron's audience refused.

phrases.term: Calling it after the land of their fathers' nativity
phrases.text: The Lamanites named their capital Jerusalem. They had kept the memory of where the family came from, and they built a city to honor it. The detail complicates any picture of them as people who forgot everything.

phrases.term: The Lamanites of themselves were sufficiently hardened
phrases.text: Mormon grades the hardness. The Lamanites were hard enough already, and the dissenters made them harder on purpose. He is careful to assign the initiative to the men who had once known better.

phrases.term: Hast thou seen an angel? Why do not angels appear unto us?
phrases.text: The Amalekite's opening question, and it is a fair one on its face. Aaron's brother Ammon had an angel; so had Alma. The man in the synagogue wants to know why the evidence is distributed the way it is, and Aaron never answers this part.

phrases.term: How knowest thou that we have cause to repent?
phrases.text: Three questions in a row press the same point: what gives a stranger standing to diagnose us. The challenge is about authority to judge, raised by a man who has already decided the answer.

phrases.term: We have built sanctuaries, and we do assemble ourselves together to worship God
phrases.text: The defense rests on attendance and construction. Both claims are true. The Amalekite offers a building program and a meeting schedule as proof of standing before God.

phrases.term: We do believe that God will save all men
phrases.text: Nehor's doctrine, quoted by his followers in a foreign country. Alma 1:4 has him preaching that all mankind should be saved at the last day. Jacob's version in 2 Nephi 9 attaches a condition: Christ saves all men who will hearken to his voice.

phrases.term: We do not believe in these foolish traditions
phrases.text: The Amalekite rejects his own fathers along with Aaron's. He says plainly that neither set of ancestors knew anything about what was coming. Alma 20 had Lamoni's father dismissing Nephites as liars; here the dissenters dismiss everybody.

phrases.term: Aaron began to open the scriptures unto them
phrases.text: The verb implies a text in hand and a reader walking others through it. He covers the coming of Christ, the resurrection, and the atonement of his blood in a single verse of summary. The mocking begins the moment he expounds.

phrases.term: Thus they were delivered for the first time out of prison
phrases.text: Mormon numbers the deliverance, which tells the reader more are coming. Fifteen verses cover a full mission, a jailing, and a rescue, and the summary ends by noting that they went straight back out.

phrases.term: That they were a free people, that they were free from the oppressions of the king, his father
phrases.text: Lamoni announces to his subjects what Ammon negotiated at swordpoint. Their freedom came from a bargain struck on a road that none of them witnessed, and the next verse turns it into a right to worship anywhere in his lands.

verses.label: v. 1–4
verses.title: Aaron goes to Jerusalem
verses.text: The brothers separate. Aaron takes the Lamanite city named for Lehi's home, built by Lamanites, Amalekites, and Amulonites. Mormon explains who is hardening whom, and notes that the synagogues follow the order of the Nehors.

verses.label: v. 5–8
verses.title: The challenge in the synagogue
verses.text: An Amalekite interrupts. Have you seen an angel, why not us, are we not as good as your people, how do you know our hearts, we have sanctuaries, God will save all men. Aaron asks one question back about the Son of God, and the man rejects the traditions of both their fathers.

verses.label: v. 9–10
verses.title: The scriptures opened, and mocked
verses.text: Aaron teaches the coming of Christ, the resurrection, and the atonement. They grow angry and refuse to listen, and he leaves without further argument.

verses.label: v. 11–15
verses.title: Ani-Anti to prison
verses.text: He finds Muloki and Ammah in a village and they contend with many. The people harden; the group moves to Middoni; a few believe. Aaron and some others are jailed until Lamoni and Ammon get them out, fed and clothed, and they go back to work.

verses.label: v. 16–17
verses.title: The second circuit
verses.text: Now they go where the Spirit leads, into any synagogue or assembly that will admit them. The Lord blesses them, many come to the truth, and many are convinced that their fathers' traditions were wrong.

verses.label: v. 18–22
verses.title: Ishmael made free
verses.text: Ammon and Lamoni come home. Lamoni refuses to let Ammon serve him, builds synagogues, gathers the people, and tells them they are free of his father and may worship where they choose in his kingdom.

verses.label: v. 23
verses.title: Ammon's daily work
verses.text: He teaches everything pertaining to righteousness and exhorts them every day with all diligence. The chapter ends with a people who give heed and are zealous to keep the commandments.

chapter.title: Mormon rewinds to show the cost
chapter.text: The reader already knows from Alma 20 that Aaron came out of prison. This chapter goes back to supply what it took to get there, so that the rescue in Alma 20 lands with weight behind it.

chapter.title: The hardest ground was Nephite
chapter.text: The Lamanites Aaron meets are hardened; the men who make them worse are dissenters who once had the record and left it. The chapter locates the deepest opposition inside the family.

chapter.title: The Amalekite's questions are good ones badly used
chapter.text: Why do angels appear to some and not others is a real question. He asks it to shut down a conversation, and the record lets it stand unanswered while it shows what he does with the answer he already had.

chapter.title: Buildings are offered as evidence and treated as none
chapter.text: The sanctuaries were real and the assemblies happened. Mormon reports the claim without disputing the facts and lets the next verse, about what they believe, do the work.

chapter.title: Aaron preaches the atonement and gets nothing
chapter.text: Alma 21 puts the fullest doctrine in the shortest summary and follows it with anger and mockery. The chapter refuses to make faithful preaching and visible success the same thing.

chapter.title: Two brothers, two results, one report
chapter.text: Ammon has a kingdom converting; Aaron has cords and a cell. Mormon writes them into adjacent chapters and assigns the difference to the people rather than to the men.

chapter.title: Deliverance is numbered and passed over
chapter.text: Verse 15 calls it the first time out of prison and moves on. The record treats rescue as an episode in a working life instead of the end of a story.

chapter.title: Religious liberty enters as a king's decree
chapter.text: Lamoni tells his people they may worship where they wish. It is a grant from above, won by a bargain, and the record notes it as a fact of the new kingdom.

applications.title: Preach where you are, then move
applications.text: Aaron argued in the synagogue, saw they would not hear, and left for the next village without escalating. When a conversation has closed, going somewhere else is a faithful response.

applications.title: Check what you are offering as evidence
applications.text: The Amalekite listed his buildings and his attendance. Write down what you would name if someone asked why you think you are right with God, and see whether the list is made of activities.

applications.title: Answer the question actually asked
applications.text: Aaron responded to a volley of challenges with one question about the Son of God. When you are being argued at from six directions, pick the one thing that matters and ask about that.

applications.title: Publish the freedom you were given
applications.text: Lamoni told his people what had been won for them and what it meant they could now do. Where someone secured something for you, make sure the people it covers know they have it.

questions.text: What piece of my own history have I kept the name of and lost the meaning of?
Who around me is hardened, and who has been working at it?
Have I asked God a real question and then refused the answer when it came in a form I did not choose?
If someone asked why I have no cause to repent, what would I say?
When did I last open the scriptures with someone rather than quote at them?
What have I counted as a first deliverance, and did I go back to work after it?
What am I zealous about keeping?
